title: What went through your mind?
subtitle: Learn the thought–action loop before trying it yourself.
description: A symptom can prompt a thought, a feeling, and an action. The thought may be understandable without being the only possible explanation. Reframing means finding a balanced response—not telling yourself that everything is fine.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.description: Imagine an agreed walk brings on familiar discomfort that settles as expected. The first thought is, 'I've made it worse.' Worry follows, and the person considers cancelling the next walk. A more balanced thought is, 'That was uncomfortable, but it settled as we discussed. I can repeat the agreed amount and review the response.' This example does not apply to a new injury or concerning change.

fields.label: What changes when the person uses the more balanced explanation?
fields.placeholder: Think about the next action—not whether they can make every worry disappear.

sections.title: Try it in your own words
sections.description: Use a familiar situation, or the example above if that is more useful. You do not need to invent a fear or disclose something personal. New or concerning symptoms should lead to appropriate advice, not an attempt to think them away.

fields.label: What was the first thought, and what is a more balanced response?
fields.placeholder: For example: 'This will ruin my week' → 'I can review the situation and choose one manageable next step.'

sections.title: Build your toolbox
sections.description: A useful response could be repeating a manageable activity, adjusting the amount, using a calming tool, or asking for guidance. Choose from the situation and your clinical plan.

fields.label: What would you do next—and why?
fields.placeholder: It is okay to be unsure. Write the question you would like help with instead.

successMessage: Reflection complete. Keep your observations in mind for your next appointment.
